Results for the half year ended 30 September 2026
Delivering on strategic objectives. Even stronger foundations for future EPS growth.
Mark Allan, Chief Executive of Landsec, commented:

“We have continued to deliver on our strategic objectives over the past six months, strengthening our positioning for a higher inflation, higher rate environment. As a result, we have further improved our near-term EPS growth outlook, our medium-term income growth potential, and our strong capital base.

“In a more uncertain world, the characteristics of our earnings matter. We own scarce, prime real assets where customer demand is concentrating. Those assets are already generating strong rental growth, with significant further income growth embedded in our portfolio. Combined with our long-dated financing, efficient cost base, and substantially completed development capex, that gives us both resilience today and visibility on an acceleration in EPS growth ahead. Our progress over the past six months further reinforces our potential to deliver c. 5% CAGR in EPRA EPS to FY30.”

Delivering on our objectives; well-placed for an acceleration in EPS growth

The past six months have been another period of successful delivery against our strategic objectives. We have continued to strengthen the quality of our best-in-class portfolio, deliver market-leading operational performance, and lower our risk profile through our clear strategic discipline. In doing this, we have further improved our near-term EPS outlook, medium-term income growth potential and sector-leading capital base, improving the visibility on the potential c. 5% CAGR in EPS by FY30 we set out previously. Despite the continuing volatility in the external environment, the trends which underpin our performance remain well-established, so the outlook for Landsec remains positive.
The high quality of our portfolio and operating platforms has again been evident over the last six months:
      Our growth in like-for-like net rental income increased to 6.2%, ahead of our c. 3-5% guidance, which means we have now delivered 4.3% CAGR in like-for-like net income over the last 4.5 years;
      Our EPRA occupancy is close to the highest level in two decades, at 97.6%;

      Our rental uplifts on relettings/renewals have increased to 16%, up from 10% a year ago, underlining the growing reversion and future income growth potential within our portfolio, with ERVs up another 2.9% over the six months;
      Our recently completed office developments are now 88% let or under offer compared to 54% in May, which will add another £13m of net rental income on an annualised basis.
Meanwhile, our strategic and capital discipline is evident in our positioning today:

      Last month we raised £500m of new equity and invested £611m in the acquisition of Metrocentre and an additional stake in Bluewater, two top-10 retail destinations in the UK. This enhances our portfolio quality, is accretive to EPS in the first year, and improves our income growth over the medium term. It also reduced our ND/EBITDA by 0.5x, so on a pro-forma basis this is now down to 7.7x;

      Our development exposure will be down to c. 2% of our portfolio by March, with no plans to add much to this in the next c. 18 months as risks around returns on prospective future projects remain elevated;
      Our overhead costs are down 29% over the last four years and remain at the lowest level in over 20 years, ensuring our income growth flows through to earnings and dividends effectively;

      Benefitting from AA credit ratings, our 8.1-year average debt maturity is twice as long as the average for the UK REIT sector and of our average 3.8% in-place cost of debt, 87% is fixed or hedged, which protects our earnings from fluctuations in interest rates.

As a result of our actions, Landsec is positioned with an even lower risk profile and clearer growth outlook than six months ago. Supported by an even stronger capital base, our increased top line income growth is set to flow through to an acceleration in EPS growth, both in the near and medium term:
      For FY27, we continue to expect EPRA EPS to be stable vs FY26 as our c. 4% underlying growth is offset by the 4% impact of last year’s sale of QAM;

      For FY28, we expect EPRA EPS to grow by an improved high-single-digit percentage, as our recent retail acquisitions add to the expected growth in earnings from leasing up our London office development pipeline and capturing the growing reversion in our existing portfolio;

      For FY30, we have improved visibility on the potential for EPRA EPS to grow to c. 62 pence, implying c. 5% CAGR from FY26. The earnings impact of the recent rise in swap rates is mitigated by our long debt maturity and higher income growth as our reversion continues to grow, so following our recent retail acquisitions, c. 90% of this c. 5% CAGR is now derived from our existing portfolio and platform.

Our financial results for the first six months of the year were positive. We delivered 6.2% growth in like-for-like net rental income and a further 9% reduction in overhead costs, which offset the 5.0% earnings impact from the sale of QAM in the second half of the prior year. As a result, EPRA EPS was effectively stable at 25.9 pence (HY25: 25.8 pence), in line with our guidance for the full year, whilst our interim dividend was up 2.1% to 19.4 pence. IFRS profit before tax rose to £243m as our leasing activity drove 2.9% growth in ERVs, resulting in a positive revaluation result. In both office and retail, occupational markets continue to be characterised by two consistent trends: a clear and sustained concentration of demand on the very best space, combined with heavy constraints on new supply. These trends have a long way to run, so as a result, the growth in rents for our best-in-class portfolios continues.

In retail, 87% of our assets sit in the top 1% of retail destinations in the UK which provide brands with access to c. 31% of national in-store retail spend. Sales growth in our locations has outperformed the UK national average by 24ppt over the past 4.5 years, with the gap widening further over the last six months. As such, our destinations remain the ones brands are focusing on in terms of investing in fewer, bigger, better stores in the best locations. New supply remains zero, as replacement costs are around double existing values, so with occupancy in our portfolio at a two-decade high, rents continue to rise.

In office, our portfolio is similarly concentrated on the very best space. We own c. 0.5% of the c. 900m sq ft of total office space in the UK. Virtually all of this is located in the two most prized locations in Europe, the West End and City of London, including Bankside. These locations are highly sought after by international businesses because of the depth of access they provide to the very best global talent. And even within these prime locations we are outperforming, with occupancy of 97.7% versus 93.7% for the central London market as a whole. Again, new supply is constrained with build cost inflation and higher interest rates limiting development viability, so as new projects are being deferred and the fit-out costs businesses face on relocating have risen sharply, rents for our high quality assets are rising.

In a world which continues to evolve rapidly, our unique and irreplaceable edge remains clear: we have two market-leading platforms and our portfolio is focused squarely at the top end of the market where customer demand is strongest. Our portfolio is virtually full, rents continue to grow, and our reversionary potential is up to a new high, so the outlook for like-for-like income growth has become even stronger.

Following an encouraging start to 2026, supported by the positive outlook for occupational markets and a stabilisation in interest rate outlook, the material increase in interest rates since the start of the Iran conflict has meant that the growing momentum in investment markets has slowed.

In offices, investors remain highly confident in the outlook for rents so demand is focused on opportunities which allow for capturing rental growth through near-term lease events or asset repositioning. Demand for stabilised assets and larger lot sizes is more sensitive to interest rates, so activity levels in this part of the market are likely to remain more subdued until the volatility in interest rates settles down. In major retail, investment activity has been more resilient given the higher day-one income yields. Despite a number of larger transactions, there are still c. £3bn of assets in the hands of parties who are not natural long term owners, so we still expect these will likely come to market in the next year or two.

Whilst recycling capital is an important part of our strategy, we are not reliant on this to drive EPS growth. Even without meaningful disposals or acquisitions from here, we could still deliver c. 90% of the potential c. 5% CAGR in EPS by FY30 and net debt/EBITDA would still fall below 7x. Moreover, committed capex is down to just £133m, so we are not reliant on disposals to fund future commitments. This means we will remain disciplined on price, especially since the outlook for rents for our best-in-class assets continues to improve now that higher interest rates and inflation are further constraining new supply.
Executing on our clear priorities in terms of capital allocation

We maintain our clear framework for capital allocation decisions as we execute our strategy. Alongside our view on risk, this is based on two factors. Firstly, how our investments contribute to income and EPS growth in the near term, and secondly, how they impact our portfolio mix such that this growth can be sustained in the medium to longer term. We prioritise investments that deliver on both factors but beyond that, our decisions will always seek to enhance at least one of these, without distracting from the other.

Based on this framework, we have sold or exchanged contracts to sell £1.0bn of assets since our strategy update in February 2025, including £338m since the start of this year. The latter included a £63m pre-development asset which had a negative in-place income return and would have required roughly £400m capex to develop; a £211m older office block where income growth over the next five years is expected to be below inflation, as a material part will be vacated shortly and will therefore require meaningful capex; and £64m of smaller non-core assets. We will continue to recycle more capital from offices and pre-development assets if opportunities arise, as the upside from reinvesting in higher-yielding, higher-growth major retail destinations remains very attractive.

The above framework also underpinned last month’s acquisitions of Metrocentre and a further 10% stake in Bluewater for a combined £611m, part-funded by a £500m equity raise. We said in May that growing our investment in major retail destinations remained our highest conviction call, but that we are disciplined on quality and price and that maintaining our strong capital base would remain our first priority. These transactions delivered on all of this: Metrocentre and Bluewater are both top-10 retail destinations in the UK; the blended 7.9% net yield means they are EPS accretive in the first year; the expected c. 4.5-7% CAGR in net rental income is accretive to our overall income growth over the medium term; and part-funding this with new equity reduced our ND/EBITDA by 0.5x and LTV by 1.0ppt.

Our near-term focus remains on further investment in retail, which we see as more attractive than starting new office or residential development. As part of our capital allocation framework, we also continue to monitor the option of deploying capital in our own shares, but for now investment in major retail is more accretive from both a near-term and longer term perspective, as the above transactions demonstrate.

Our three recently completed London office developments are now 88% let or under offer, with strong interest in the remaining space. Completion of our fourth office scheme, Thirty High, has been delayed by up to six months due to an issue which arose during testing and commissioning. This has been resolved since then and as the effect on leasing timelines is less pronounced, there is no material impact on cost or our earnings guidance. As we have no plans to commit significant further capital to speculative office development at this stage, committed development exposure will come down to less than 2% of our portfolio by the year-end.

In residential, we have concluded that the risk/return prospects of our proposed development plans at Lewisham are not sufficiently attractive whilst the opportunity cost of deferring retail asset management initiatives was rising. As such, we will no longer pursue redevelopment and instead focus on enhancing the existing shopping centre and growing income from that. However, at Finchley Road we secured a revised planning consent which materially improves development viability, whilst at Mayfield, we continue the constructive engagement with our public sector partners to find similar opportunities for viability improvements. We are mindful that the external environment continues to evolve but for now we are continuing to invest the necessary time in both schemes as capex requirements remain limited for the next 12-18 months.

Above all, maintaining our strong capital base remains our first priority. With pro-forma ND/EBITDA of 7.7x on track to reduce to comfortably below 7x and our development exposure set to come down to minimal levels, we are continuing to move towards a materially lower risk profile.

Owning the right real estate is more crucial than ever. Driven by the highly talented teams across our two best-in-class platforms, the operational performance across our office and retail portfolios, which including our latest transactions now make up 92% of our overall income, remains market-leading.

The delivery against our strategic objectives since the start of the year means we have further improved our near-term EPS growth outlook, medium term income growth potential, and capital base. We have now delivered CAGR in like-for-like net rental income of 4.3% over the last 4.5 years and as our reversion has grown to new highs, the future income growth potential embedded in our business remains significant. As our overhead costs are at a 20-year low, our development exposure is minimal, and our average debt maturity is twice the sector average, this top line income growth will flow through to an acceleration in EPS growth over the coming years, supporting continued growth in dividends.

We are mindful that global macro risks remain elevated, yet the trends which have supported our strong operational performance continue to have good momentum. As a result of our actions since the start of the year, our business now has a lower risk profile and clearer growth outlook than it had six months ago. Our ND/EBITDA is down to 7.7x and the visibility of the potential c. 5% CAGR in EPRA EPS by FY30, including high single digit growth in FY28, has improved further. Combined with our high quality current income return, this will result in an attractive total return for shareholders.

Over time, income growth is the main driver of value growth in both real estate and equity markets. As such, the overarching objective of our strategy is to deliver sustainable growth in income and EPS, both in the near and long term. In turn, this will drive an attractive return on equity for shareholders.

To deliver this, we have created an irreplaceable, high quality real estate portfolio which produces £652m of annualised rental income, or £685m including acquisitions and disposals post the period-end. The latter principally comprises office-led places (47% of income), focused principally on a small number of high-amenity, well-connected key locations in the West End and City & Southwark, and our retail-led destinations (45% of income), 87% of which sit in the top 1% highest selling retail locations in the UK.

This portfolio is highly reversionary and therefore offers material future income growth. Combined with our market-leading operating platforms, efficient overhead cost base and long-duration debt book, this is what underpins our EPS growth in the near term. Our decisions on future capital recycling and deployment are about making sure that in a few years’ time, our asset mix is such that we are still as confident about the income growth prospects of our portfolio as we are today.
Capturing reversion and driving like-for-like income growth

We have delivered another period of strong like-for-like net rental income growth, as growth accelerated to 6.2%, up from 4.6% in FY26, with high growth in both offices and retail. Occupancy remains close to the two decade-high of 98.0% we reported in March, down 40bps due to a reduction in occupancy in offices toward the end of the period, with rental uplifts on relettings/renewals across the two main parts of our portfolio of 16%. On a like-for-like basis, our gross to net margin was up 1.2ppt. Growth in ERVs was 2.9% for the six months, which adds to the embedded income growth in our portfolio.

Demand for high quality office space in locations that offer the right amenities and transport connectivity remains high. As new supply is set to be modest in the next few years, with higher interest rates and cost inflation weighing on development economics, this means rents continue to grow. Moreover, as fit-out costs are up almost 60% over the past five years, we are seeing more customers opting to stay when their existing space is of the right quality, unless their space requirements change.

Our EPRA occupancy reduced 90bps to 97.7% as at the end of September, principally reflecting lease expiries at our only asset in Paddington towards the end of the period. Since the period-end, we have agreed new lettings adding 30bps to occupancy, so our occupancy remains well ahead of the Central London market at 93.7%.

During the first half of the year, we completed 18 lettings and renewals totalling £7m of rent, on average 5% ahead of ERV, with another £2m of lettings in solicitors’ hands, 16% above ERV. Uplifts on relettings and renewals during the half year were 18%, so alongside growth in Myo income and upside from rent reviews, this drove 5.4% LFL net rental income growth. ERV growth over the first six months was 3.4%, so our reversionary potential rose to 20%. As the outlook for ERV growth remains positive, we expect this will support slightly higher LFL income growth over the next few years than previously envisaged.

Occupancy across our stabilised Myo portfolio increased from 84% to 97% and rents achieved were in line with budget. Including our new Kings Cross location which opened a year ago and is now 98% let, Myo now makes up 7% of our income in our office-led business.

The top 1% of all UK shopping destinations provide access to c. 31% of the country’s in-store, non-food retail spend, offering brands higher sales densities and productivity than other formats. Including our acquisitions since the period-end, c. 87% of our retail assets sit in this top 1%, which underpins their continued outperformance. Total sales across our portfolio were up 3.7% vs the prior year, with footfall up 1.6% - both materially ahead of the UK national benchmarks of -1.4% and 0.1% respectively, as our locations continue to gain market share.

Since FY22, sales growth across our portfolio has outperformed the UK national average by a cumulative 24ppt and this gap continues to widen, whilst our 8% footfall growth over the last few years means we continue to grow our market share. Including our recent acquisitions, our overall annual footfall is now close to 190 million and we have a consumer reach of one in three people in the UK, providing brands with access to more footfall and a larger consumer reach than any other retail platform in the UK. Supported by the unique data and insights this offers us, we continue to invest in creating the best experience, creating a virtuous circle of growing footfall driving higher sales, which in turn attract the best brands, which then attract more footfall, and so on.

The success of this approach is translating into an acceleration in income growth. Occupancy increased a further 10bps since March to 97.8%, which is the highest level in over 20 years. We signed 105 leases totalling £15m of rent on average 4% above ERV, which supported 2.3% ERV growth over six months. Rental uplifts vs previous passing rent on relettings and renewals were 15% and have increased further since, underlining the growing reversionary potential in our portfolio. Combined with growth in turnover income, this meant like-for-like net rental income growth increased to 6.3% from 5.5% in FY26.

Our leasing pipeline is even stronger, with £14m of lettings in solicitors’ hands on average 21% ahead of ERV and, in the case of relettings and renewals, 18% above previous passing rent. With our portfolio essentially full and zero new supply, we are very well-placed to deliver the 4.5-7% CAGR in income we target over the coming years. This reflects a mix of capturing the growing reversion across our portfolio and growth in turnover income (3-4%); growth in commercialisation income such as digital media, events and EV charging (0.5-1%); and a c. £200m investment in smaller, accretive capex projects (1-2%).

The income in this part of our portfolio currently solely reflects the income on our existing retail assets at Finchley Road and Lewisham. The latter is expected to grow meaningfully in the next few years now that we are no longer pursuing its residential redevelopment. Overall, like-for-like net income was up £1m.
LFL occupancy across our residual retail and leisure parks was up 40bps to 97.4% and like-for-like income for the period was up 3.0%, driven by our positive leasing activity.
Releasing capital from lower returning assets

With £1.0bn of disposals over the past c. 18 months, including £338m since the start of this financial year, we have made strong progress on the objective to release c. £3bn of capital over a five-year period from lower-returning offices, retail/leisure parks and pre-development assets we set out in February 2025.

Our largest disposal this year was the sale of 123 Victoria Street in October for £211m. This 1970’s office block was last refurbished in 2012 and whilst it is currently fully let, around one-third will become vacant in 2027, at which point it will require meaningful capex. As such, our five-year income return on the asset was expected to be c. 6.0%, with income growth over this period expected to be below inflation. The receipt of £30m of the proceeds is deferred for up to 36 months, yet this will generate 6.0% interest p.a.

As part of our objective to reduce our capital employed in pre-development assets we sold a site in the City, releasing £63m of capital which generated a net income yield of -0.3%. We will act as development manager for the project, which will allow us to leverage our development skillset and expertise through fee income without having to commit c. £400m of our own balance sheet capital to deliver this scheme. We expect to release more capital from pre-development assets over the next 6-12 months. In addition, we have exchanged contracts to sell a £46m leisure asset and we sold £18m of smaller non-core assets. Overall, our disposals release £338m of capital from assets which generated limited income or income growth. Combined, these disposals are marginally accretive to EPS at a limited 0.6% cost to NTA.
Investing in higher income, higher growth acquisitions

We have a clear track-record in growing our investment in major retail destinations, having delivered a 15% unlevered IRR and 14% income growth on the £0.9bn we invested in major retail acquisitions in recent years so far. We have continued to build on this, as shortly after the period-end we acquired a 100% stake in Metrocentre, located two miles outside Newcastle city centre. Metrocentre is one of the top-10 retail destinations in the UK by sales and home to a wide range of leading international brands. It is the dominant retail destination in the north-east, with sales performance for key brands in the centre on average c. 30-35% higher than in their stores in Newcastle city centre.

The net consideration of £516m represented an in-place net rental income yield of 7.9%. We expect this yield to improve by c. 40bps in the short term due to the cost efficiencies of integrating this into our own operating platform. In addition, we expect to deliver CAGR in net rental income in line with the c. 4.5-7% target for our existing portfolio. This is driven by a number of similar asset management initiatives as we have successfully deployed elsewhere in our portfolio, for which we expect to invest c. £30m in capex.

Last month we also acquired an additional 10% stake in Bluewater for £95m, representing a 7.4% net rental income yield. Aside from the attractive income return for one of the top-10 retail destinations in the UK, this offers further benefits in the form of improved efficiency and operational flexibility, as it materially simplifies the ownership structure and takes our stake in the asset to 74%. Combined with two small acquisitions during the first half of the year, this brings total acquisitions to date to £633m.
Development and investments in our existing assets

Our investment in capex halved vs the same period last year as our office developments are substantially complete, we have reduced capex on pre-development assets, and delivered more efficiencies across the rest of our portfolio. In total, we invested £119m in capex, comprising £44m for our on-site office projects in Victoria and Manchester, £14m in pre-development assets, and £61m across our operational portfolio, including £30m for smaller projects, leasing and maintenance in retail, and £31m across our offices.

We continue to see strong demand at our three recently completed London office developments so these are now 88% let or under offer, up from 54% in May, with positive leasing driving further growth in ERV. Our major project at Timber Square (£34m ERV) which completed in March is now 89% let or under offer (was 54%) whilst Myo Kings Cross (£10m ERV) is now 98% let (was 75%) and our small office in Oval (£4m ERV) is 55% let or under offer (was 10%). With good interest in the remaining space, this is consistent with our assumption that our projects will lease up within c. 12 months post completion.

Completion of our latest London office project, Thirty High (£36m ERV), has been delayed by up to six months due to an issue which arose during testing and commissioning. This has now been resolved and the impact of this on leasing timing is less significant as we can commence fit-out works ahead of the revised completion date. As such, we do not expect this to have a material impact on EPS guidance or TDC. The building is 11% under offer and we have active customer interest for over 80% of the space.

Our leasing progress over the past six months will add an additional £14m of annual net rental income to the £21m we had already secured, leaving £31m of net effective rent to lease, principally at Thirty High and the two remaining floors at Timber Square. Combined, this will drive high growth in income in FY28 and more than offset the fact that interest will no longer be capitalised on projects post completion. As such, this supports our outlook for strong growth in earnings next year.

Following the completion of Thirty High, our committed development exposure will come down to £0.2bn, as our only committed office project is our £155m development at Mayfield, Manchester. We are also on site with £32m of smaller retail projects, such as the creation of a new social eating destination at Trinity, Leeds and enhancing the central square at Gunwharf Quays. Combined, these smaller retail projects are expected to generate highly accretive, low double-digit yields on cost.

Based on our capital allocation framework, investment in major retail destinations remains most attractive in our view, both from a near as well as medium term impact on income and EPS. As such, we do not plan to commit any meaningful balance sheet capital to new development for the next c. 18 months.

For new office development, we believe returns do not offer sufficient upside relative to the returns we expect on our high quality existing office assets. Whilst higher rental growth could improve development returns, we would also benefit from this market growth via our existing £7bn office portfolio. Taking into account the higher level of risk in development, this means we see little upside in selling our high quality existing offices to redeploy the same balance sheet capital into funding the development of new ones. Still, we will continue to invest in our existing portfolio, e.g. via the £38m planned investment in one of our assets at New Street Square, which includes the retrofit of air source heat pumps and public realm improvements for the overall estate, to capitalise on the demand for high quality space across this estate.

In residential, longer-term characteristics remain attractive given the persistent demand-supply imbalance and low cyclicality. However, current development returns are challenged by higher interest rates, rising exit yields and cost inflation. We have made good progress on improving the development viability of our c. 1,800-unit scheme at Finchley Road, north London, with resolution to grant an improved planning consent, which amongst others reduces the share of affordable housing provision from 35% to 20%. At our c. 1,700-unit scheme at Mayfield, next to Manchester’s main train station, we continue our constructive engagement with public sector partners to improve the viability of this project.

Alongside this progress, we are mindful that the external environment continues to evolve. As both our current capital employed and near-term capex requirements for both sites is low, we believe it is worth continuing to invest the necessary time to pursue viability. Taking into account detailed design works, Building Safety Act approvals, and site preparation, the earliest starts would not be before 2028 in any event. Meanwhile, we have decided that we will not pursue our potential residential redevelopment at Lewisham, as the risk/return prospects of the scheme were not sufficiently attractive and the opportunity cost of deferring alternative, retail-focused asset management initiatives was rising. As leasing at the existing shopping centre will no longer be held back by the redevelopment plans, we will now focus on growing its long-term income, taking advantage of its significant c. 13m annual footfall.

Irrespective of sectors, we are mindful of the negative impact on our risk profile and EPS growth of having large amounts of capital tied up in development for prolonged periods. Looking forward, we will therefore keep our exposure to committed development closer to about half of the c. £1bn it has been over the last five years via a combination of lower activity levels and working with capital partners on certain projects, as we have done with one of our office development projects in the City this year.

Delivering sustainable income growth will underpin growth in property values over time, yet in the short term values are also affected by changes in valuation yields. Our leasing activity resulted in ERV growth of 2.9% over the last six months, with overall values up 0.8% over the half year. Office values were broadly unchanged, with 3.4% ERV growth offset by slight yield softening, whereas retail values were up, driven by 2.3% ERV growth and generally stable yields. The valuation of our future residential developments was down modestly, whilst our residual retail and leisure parks were largely stable.

Best-in-class assets which are seeing strong occupational demand and hence offer clear income growth continue to look attractive relative to real interest rates, despite the increase in nominal interest rates. That said, we are mindful that persistent volatility in global bond markets could continue to weigh on investor decision-making and with that, result in a softening in valuation yields. For our portfolio however, we expect the impact of this on valuations to be mitigated by further ERV growth, as high customer demand means we continue to expect ERVs to grow by a mid-single digit percentage this year.

Growing income and EPS in a sustainable way

As we grow income and EPS, it is important our growth is sustainable in all aspects. We target to reduce direct and indirect greenhouse gas emissions by 47% by 2030 vs 2019/20, including all of our Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions, and to reach net zero by 2040. Our emissions are now down 46% vs our 2019/20 baseline, driven by significant improvements in the UK electricity grid decarbonisation, the retrofit of air source heat pumps in offices, and our reduced development exposure.

As part of our objective to reduce our energy intensity, we are introducing AI smart building technology across over 20 of our assets to transform how they are managed and experienced. The automation and intelligent diagnostics this provides enables smarter decision making on energy management, which has driven a meaningful reduction in energy consumption and energy costs for the 15 properties where this technology is already live.

In 2021, we set out a net zero transition investment plan to ensure all our assets would meet a Minimum Energy Efficiency Standard of EPC ‘B’ by 2030. The cost of this is reflected in our valuations and having already completed the retrofit of air source heat pumps at six of our buildings, we are now on site with our latest retrofit at 80-100 Victoria Street and will shortly start works at 6 New Street Square. 71% of our overall portfolio is now rated EPC ‘B’ or higher, up from 68% in March. In office, 73% of our portfolio is rated EPC ‘B’ or higher which is expected to increase further following completion of Thirty High and 80-100 Victoria Street retrofit. As such, we are on track to achieve our objective.

Finally, via our Landsec Futures programme, we continue to improve social mobility in real estate and tackle issues local to our assets. To date, this has created career pathways for 24 interns and supported 14 real estate bursaries. From our 2019/20 baseline, we have so far created £166m of social value and empowered 20,909 people towards the world of work.

Our financial results have been underpinned by our continued strong operational performance. EPRA earnings were stable at £192m, as the £10m earnings impact from the sale of QAM during the second half of the prior year was offset by our 6.2% growth in like-for-like income. We also delivered additional cost efficiencies, so our overhead costs remain at the lowest level in over 20 years.

As a result, EPRA EPS was essentially stable at 25.9 pence (+0.4%), in line with our guidance for the full year and our interim dividend is up 2.1% to 19.4 pence, in line with our policy of a 1.2-1.3x dividend cover on an annual basis. The strong performance of our leasing and asset management teams not only meant our like-for-like income growth was ahead of our c. 3-5% guidance for the full year, but also drove 2.9% ERV growth over six months. This resulted in a positive revaluation result, which meant IFRS profit before tax increased to £243m and NTA per share as at September was up 1.2% vs March, at 893 pence.

We have also further improved our strong capital base. Post the period-end we issued 83m new shares, raising £500m new equity to fund the £611m acquisitions of Metrocentre and a further stake in Bluewater – both of which are top-10 retail destinations in the UK, with an accretive in-place income yield and strong income growth prospects. Combined with £338m of disposals, this means pro-forma net debt/EBITDA is down from 8.4x to 7.7x and our LTV is down from 38.7% to 37.1%, whilst NTA per share is 863 pence.

As we are not planning to start any meaningful new developments in the near future, we are on track to see net debt/EBITDA reduce to comfortably below 7x as we continue to lease up the rest of our recent developments and capture the reversion in our existing portfolio. Meanwhile, our AA credit rating and 8.1-year average debt maturity are the highest in the UK REIT sector, whilst our 3.8% in-place interest cost is 87% fixed or hedged for a similar period. With just £133m committed development capex left and development exposure set to come down to less than 2% of our portfolio, this means our risk profile is well below the sector average. The stability this provides underpins our positive EPS growth outlook and with that, the attractive return on equity prospects for shareholders.

For FY27, we continue to expect EPRA EPS to be stable vs the 51.4 pence in FY26 as underlying growth is offset by the 4% full-year impact of the sale of QAM. For FY28, we expect EPS to grow by an improved high single digit percentage, as our recent retail acquisitions add to the growth in EPS from leasing up our London office development pipeline and continued like-for-like income growth. Although the rise in global interest rates since May is expected to increase our future refinancing cost, the impact of this on earnings is offset by our long debt maturity and higher like-for-like income growth than we had previously assumed, mostly in offices, as our reversion continues to grow. As such, we continue to see the potential for EPS to grow to c. 62 pence by FY30. This implies c. 5% CAGR in EPS over FY27-30, of which c. 90% is now driven by our current portfolio and platform, up from c. 80% six months ago.

Maintaining our strong capital base remains a key priority for us. Whilst we consider a range of measures on this front, we increasingly view net debt/EBITDA as a more appropriate leverage measure than LTV. The reasons for this are that unlike LTV, net debt/EBITDA is a true cash-on-cash measure; is not reliant on inherently subjective valuations; and is taking into account other factors which impact financial risk, such as development exposure and the associated leasing risk.

Our capital operating guidelines are to have a net debt/EBITDA of less than 8x, an LTV within a 25-40% range, and an ICR of at least 3x. Taking into account the acquisitions, disposals and equity issue we concluded after the period-end, we are comfortably within all these guidelines.

Our net debt/EBITDA and LTV were broadly stable during the half year, but have reduced to 7.7x and 37.1% respectively on a pro-forma basis since the period-end. As we have limited development capex left to spend on our current pipeline, the lease-up of our recently completed and last on-site London office development means net debt/EBITDA will come down meaningfully over the next year.

We will maintain a structurally lower level of capital employed in development in the future than we have had in recent years. Combined with continued like-for-like income growth, we therefore expect net debt/EBITDA (which we present on a proportionally consolidated basis) to reduce comfortably below 7x without having to rely on material disposals. We expect our 37.1% LTV to reduce further to below 35% over time. Reflecting our strong capital base and high quality portfolio and income profile, we benefit from AA credit ratings from both S&P and DBRS, which is the highest rating in the UK REIT sector.

The principal risks and uncertainties of the business were set out on pages 44 – 46 of the 2026 Annual Report published in June. The Executive Leadership Team and the Board review these risks regularly and continue to monitor for changes and emerging risks in the context of delivering our strategic objectives. Though the risk landscape continues to evolve and change over time, they remain the most relevant and the principal risks at the half year are unchanged from those disclosed in the Annual Report.

The macro-economic outlook remains our highest-rated principal risk and has some impact on aspects of our other strategic risks related to the office and retail occupier markets, development strategy and capital allocation. Inflation has picked up slightly and uncertainty persists around the UK fiscal outlook. The high levels of long-term interest rates and financing costs present challenges for the business; however we continue to deliver a strong operational performance, and we have the longest weighted-average debt maturity within the UK Real Estate sector.
Our nine principal risks to delivering our strategy and their current outlook are summarised as follows:

Macro-economic outlook – This risk has been updated to remove the previous references to build project uncertainty, due to our reduction in our onsite development activity. It otherwise continues to capture the potential impacts of changes in the broader economic environment, including inflationary pressures, persistently elevated interest rates and shifts in business and consumer confidence. This risk has remained stable since the year end. For Landsec this risk impacts asset yields, income and therefore valuations and our cost base. It may also create opportunities to acquire assets.

Office occupier market – The risk associated with this market is considered to have remained stable over the period. Demand continues to focus on the best quality assets in the strongest locations: both characteristics of our portfolio. As a result, our operational performance remains strong.

Retail and hospitality occupier market – The market remains very strong, and portfolio performance has benefitted over recent years from capturing growing rental reversion through lease events and turnover rents. Vacancy levels are now at their lowest level in 20 years. Whilst this reflects the strength of the portfolio and occupier demand, it also reduces the opportunity to generate further upside through vacancy reduction, albeit offset to some extent by growing reversion. Consequently, the net risk has increased slightly during the period and is now within the lower end of our defined risk appetite of ‘flexible’.

Capital allocation – This risk is considered to have increased due to the continued rise in bond yields since the year end which has weighed on investment demand in the London office market. This has been offset by tighter management of capex across the business to maintain a stable net risk position.

Development – This risk is considered to have remained stable since the year end. As the majority of the development costs of our committed schemes is already fixed, and no new development commitments are planned in the near future, this risk is expected to reduce further as our current projects complete.

Information security and cyber threat – This risk is considered to have remained stable despite the continued evolution of the external threat landscape, as we continue to focus on investing in operational strengthening to improve processes and controls in this area. This risk remains within our cautious risk appetite.
The three remaining operational principal risks (Health and safety, People and skills, and Climate change transition) have remained stable in the six months since the year end.

Given the impact of international and domestic political and economic events since 1 April 2026, the Directors have continued to place additional focus on the appropriateness of adopting the going concern assumption in preparing the financial statements for the half year ended 30 September 2026. The Group’s going concern assessment considers changes in the Group’s principal risks (see page 21) and is dependent on a number of factors, including our financial performance and continued access to borrowing facilities. Access to our borrowing facilities is also dependent on our ability to continue to operate the Group’s secured debt structure within its financial covenants, which are described in note 14.

In order to satisfy themselves that the Group has adequate resources to continue as a going concern for the foreseeable future, the Directors have reviewed base case, downside and reverse stress test models, as well as a cash flow model which considers the impact of pessimistic assumptions on the Group’s operating environment (the ‘mitigated downside scenario’). This mitigated downside scenario reflects unfavourable macroeconomic conditions, a deterioration in our ability to collect rent and service charge from our customers and removes uncommitted capital expenditure, acquisitions, disposals and developments.

The Group’s key metrics from the mitigated downside scenario as at the end of the going concern assessment period, which covers the 16 months to 31 March 2028, are shown below alongside the actual position at 30 September 2026.

In our mitigated downside scenario, the Group has sufficient cash reserves, with our Security Group LTV ratio remaining less than 65% and interest cover above 1.45x, for a period of 16 months from the date of authorisation of these financial statements. Under this scenario, the Security Group’s asset values would need to fall by a further 33% from the sensitised values forecasted at 31 March 2028 to be non‑compliant with the LTV covenant. This equates to a 35% fall in the value of the Security Group’s assets as at 30 September 2026 for the LTV to reach 65%. The Directors consider the likelihood of this occurring over the going concern assessment period to be remote.

The Security Group also requires earnings before interest of at least £252m in the full year ending 31 March 2027 and at least £315m in the full year ending 31 March 2028 for interest cover to remain above 1.45x in the mitigated downside scenario, which would ensure compliance with the Group’s covenant through to the end of the going concern assessment period. Security Group earnings post year end 31 March 2026 are above the level required to meet the interest cover covenant for the year ended 31 March 2026. The Directors do not anticipate a reduction in Security Group earnings over the period ending 31 March 2027 to a level that would result in a breach of the interest cover covenant.

The Directors have also considered a reverse stress-test scenario which assumes no further rent will be received, to determine when our available cash resources would be exhausted. Even under this extreme scenario, although breaching the interest cover covenant, the Group continues to have sufficient cash reserves to continue in operation throughout the going concern assessment period.

Based on these considerations, together with available market information and the Directors’ knowledge and experience of the Group’s property portfolio and markets, the Directors have adopted the going concern basis in preparing the financial statements of the Group for the half year ended 30 September 2026.

A number of the financial measures used internally by the Group to measure performance include the results of partly-owned subsidiaries and joint ventures on a proportionate basis. Measures that are described as being on a proportionate basis include the Group’s share of joint ventures on a line-by-line basis and are adjusted to exclude the non-owned elements of our subsidiaries. These measures are non-GAAP measures and therefore not presented in accordance with IFRS. This is in contrast to the condensed consolidated interim financial information presented in these half year results, where the Group applies equity accounting to its interest in joint ventures and associates, presenting its interest collectively in the income statement and balance sheet, and consolidating all subsidiaries at 100% with any non-owned element being adjusted as a non-controlling interest or redemption liability, as appropriate. Our joint operations are presented on a proportionate basis in all financial measures used internally by the Group.

The Group’s operations are all in the UK and are managed across four operating segments, being Office-led, Retail-led, Residential-led and Other assets.

The Office-led segment includes all operating or under development office assets in London and the regions as well as the associated retail and other premises in proximity to these assets. The Retail-led segment includes all the shopping centres and outlets in our portfolio. The Residential-led segment includes our residential developments and the Other assets segment is mainly comprised of our retail and leisure park assets.

Management has determined the Group’s operating segments based on the information reviewed by Senior Management to make strategic decisions. The chief operating decision maker is the Executive Leadership Team (ELT), comprising the Executive Directors and the Managing Directors. The information presented to ELT includes reports from all functions of the business as well as strategy, financial planning, succession planning, organisational development and Group-wide policies.

The Group’s primary measure of underlying profit before tax is EPRA earnings. However, Segment net rental income is the lowest level to which the profit arising from the ongoing operations of the Group is analysed between the four segments. The administrative costs, which are predominantly staff costs for centralised functions, are all treated as administrative expenses and are not allocated to individual segments.

The MTNs are secured on the fixed and floating pool of assets of the Security Group. The Security Group includes wholly owned investment properties, development properties and a number of the Group’s investment in additional assets, in total valued at £10.6bn at 30 September 2026 (31 March 2026: £10.4bn). The secured debt structure has a tiered operating covenant regime which gives the Group substantial flexibility when the LTV and interest cover in the Security Group are less than 65% and more than 1.45x respectively. If these limits are exceeded, the operating environment becomes more restrictive with provisions to encourage a reduction in gearing. The interest rate of each MTN is fixed until the expected maturity, being two years before the legal maturity date of the MTN. The interest rate for the last two years may either become floating on a SONIA basis plus an increased margin (relative to that at the time of issue), or subject to a fixed coupon uplift, depending on the terms and conditions of the specific notes.

The effective interest rate is based on the coupon paid and includes the amortisation of issue costs and discount to redemption value. As at 31 March 2026, the MTNs were listed on Euronext Dublin and their fair values are based on their respective market prices. As of 1 September 2026, the MTNs are now listed on the London Stock Exchange.

Adjusted net cash inflow from operating activities
Net cash inflow from operating activities including the Group’s share of our joint ventures’ net cash inflow from operating activities.

Net debt excluding cumulative fair value movements on interest-rate swaps and amounts payable under head leases. It generally includes the net debt of subsidiaries and joint ventures on a proportionate basis.

The Combined Portfolio comprises the investment properties, owner-occupied property and non-current assets held-for-sale of the Group’s subsidiaries, on a proportionately consolidated basis when not wholly owned, together with our share of investment properties held in our joint ventures.

Development pipeline consists of future developments, committed developments, projects under construction and developments which have reached practical completion within the last two years but are not yet 95% let.
Development gross yield on total development cost
Gross ERV, before adjustment for lease incentives, divided by total development cost. Gross ERV reflects Landsec’s or the valuer’s view of expected ERV at completion of the scheme.

Profit before tax, excluding profits on the sale of non-current assets and trading properties, profits on development contracts, valuation movements, fair value movements on interest-rate swaps and similar instruments used for hedging purposes, debt restructuring charges, and any other items of an exceptional nature.

Ratio of adjusted net debt, including net payables, to the sum of the net assets, including net receivables, of the Group, its subsidiaries and joint ventures, all on a proportionate basis, expressed as a percentage. The calculation includes trading properties at fair value and debt at nominal value.
EPRA net disposal value (NDV) per share

Diluted net assets per share adjusted to remove the impact of goodwill arising as a result of deferred tax, and to include the difference between the fair value and the book value of the net investment in tenant finance leases and fixed interest rate debt.

EPRA net initial yield is defined within EPRA’s Best Practice Recommendations as the annualised rental income based on the cash rents passing at the balance sheet date, less non-recoverable property operating expenses, divided by the gross market value of the property. It is consistent with the net initial yield calculated by the Group’s external valuer.
EPRA Net Reinstatement Value (NRV) per share

Diluted net assets per share adjusted to remove the cumulative fair value movements on interest-rate swaps and similar instruments, the carrying value of deferred tax on intangible assets and to include the difference between the fair value and the book value of the net investment in tenant finance leases and add back purchasers’ costs.
EPRA Net Tangible Assets (NTA) per share

Diluted net assets per share adjusted to remove the cumulative fair value movements on interest-rate swaps and similar instruments, the carrying value of goodwill arising as a result of deferred tax and other intangible assets, deferred tax on intangible assets and to include the difference between the fair value and the book value of the net investment in tenant finance leases.
Calculated as the Estimated Rental Value (ERV) of occupied space divided by the ERV of the total portfolio excluding developments.

Calculated by the Group’s external valuer, equivalent yield is the internal rate of return from an investment property, based on the gross outlays for the purchase of a property (including purchase costs), reflecting reversions to current market rent and such items as voids and non-recoverable expenditure but ignoring future changes in capital value. The calculation assumes rent is received annually in arrears.

The estimated market rental value of lettable space as determined biannually by the Group’s external valuer. For investment properties in the development programme, which have not yet reached practical completion, the ERV represents management’s view of market rents.

Total borrowings, including bank overdrafts, less short-term deposits, corporate bonds and cash, at book value, plus cumulative fair value movements on financial derivatives as a percentage of total equity. For adjusted gearing, see note 13.
Market value plus assumed usual purchaser’s costs at the reporting date.

A calculation of a company’s ability to meet its interest payments on outstanding debt. It is calculated using EPRA earnings before interest, divided by net interest (excluding the mark-to-market movement on interest-rate swaps, foreign exchange swaps, capitalised interest and interest on the pension scheme assets and liabilities). The calculation excludes joint ventures.
The investment portfolio comprises the investment properties of the Group’s subsidiaries on a proportionately consolidated basis where not wholly owned.

Any incentive offered to occupiers to enter into a lease. Typically, the incentive will be an initial rent-free period, or a cash contribution to fit-out or similar costs. For accounting purposes, the value of the incentive is spread over the non-cancellable life of the lease.

The like-for-like portfolio includes all properties which have been in the portfolio since 1 April 2023 but excluding those which are acquired or sold since that date. Properties in the development pipeline and completed developments are also excluded.

Group LTV is the ratio of adjusted net debt, including subsidiaries and joint ventures, to the sum of the market value of investment properties and the book value of trading properties of the Group, its subsidiaries and joint ventures, all on a proportionate basis, expressed as a percentage. For the Security Group, LTV is the ratio of net debt lent to the Security Group divided by the value of secured assets.

Market value is determined by the Group’s external valuer, in accordance with the RICS Valuation Standards, as an opinion of the estimated amount for which a property should exchange on the date of valuation between a willing buyer and a willing seller in an arm’s-length transaction after proper marketing.

Net initial yield is a calculation by the Group’s external valuer of the yield that would be received by a purchaser, based on the Estimated Net Rental Income expressed as a percentage of the acquisition cost, being the market value plus assumed usual purchasers’ costs at the reporting date. The calculation is in line with EPRA guidance. Estimated Net Rental Income is determined by the valuer and is based on the passing cash rent less rent payable at the balance sheet date, estimated non-recoverable outgoings and void costs including service charges, insurance costs and void rates.

Net rental income is the net operational income arising from properties, on an accruals basis, including rental income, finance lease interest, rents payable, service charge income and expense, other property related income, direct property expenditure and bad debts. Net rental income is presented on a proportionate basis.

A building for which an overall balance has been achieved between carbon emissions produced and those taken out of the atmosphere, including via offset arrangements. This relates to operational emissions for all buildings while, for a new building, it also includes supply-chain emissions associated with its construction.

The estimated annual rent receivable as at the reporting date which includes estimates of turnover rent and estimates of rent to be agreed in respect of outstanding rent review or lease renewal negotiations. Passing rent may be more or less than the ERV (see over-rented, reversionary and ERV). Passing rent excludes annual rent receivable from units in administration save to the extent that rents are expected to be received. Void units at the reporting date are deemed to have no passing rent. Although temporary lets of less than 12 months are treated as void, income from temporary lets is included in passing rents.
A PID is a distribution by a REIT to its shareholders paid out of qualifying profits. A REIT is required to distribute at least 90% of its qualifying profits as a PID to its shareholders.

Rental income is as reported in the income statement, on an accruals basis, and adjusted for the spreading of lease incentives over the term certain of the lease in accordance with IFRS 16. It is stated gross, prior to the deduction of ground rents and without deduction for operational outgoings on car park and commercialisation activities.
Space where the passing rent is below the ERV.
The anticipated yield to which the initial yield will rise (or fall) once the rent reaches the ERV.

Security Group is the principal funding vehicle for the Group and properties held in the Security Group are mortgaged for the benefit of lenders. It has the flexibility to raise a variety of different forms of finance.

Topped-up net initial yield is a calculation by the Group’s external valuer. It is calculated by making an adjustment to net initial yield in respect of the annualised cash rent foregone through unexpired rent-free periods and other lease incentives. The calculation is consistent with EPRA guidance.
Total accounting return (previously Total return on equity)
Dividend paid per share in the year plus the change in EPRA Net Tangible Assets per share, divided by EPRA Net Tangible Assets per share at the beginning of the year.

Total cost ratio represents all costs included within EPRA earnings, other than rents payable, financing costs and provisions for bad and doubtful debts, expressed as a percentage of gross rental income before rents payable adjusted for costs recovered through rents but not separately invoiced.

Total development cost refers to the book value of the site at the commencement of the project, the estimated capital expenditure required to develop the scheme from the start of the financial year in which the property is added to our development programme, together with capitalised interest, being the Group’s borrowing costs associated with direct expenditure on the property under development. Interest is also capitalised on the purchase cost of land or property where it is acquired specifically for redevelopment. The TDC for trading property development schemes excludes any estimated tax on disposal.
Properties held for trading purposes and shown as current assets in the balance sheet.

Vacancy rates are expressed as a percentage of ERV and represent all unlet space, including vacant properties where refurbishment work is being carried out and vacancy in respect of pre-development properties, unless the scale of refurbishment is such that the property is not deemed lettable. The screen at Piccadilly Lights, W1 is excluded from the vacancy rate calculation as it will always carry advertising although the number and duration of our agreements with advertisers will vary.

The valuation surplus/deficit represents the increase or decrease in the market value of the Combined Portfolio, adjusted for net investment and the effect of accounting for lease incentives under IFRS 16. The market value of the Combined Portfolio is determined by the Group’s external valuer.

Voids are expressed as a percentage of ERV and represent all unlet space, including voids where refurbishment work is being carried out and voids in respect of pre-development properties. Temporary lettings for a period of one year or less are also treated as voids. The screen at Piccadilly Lights, W1 is excluded from the void calculation as it will always carry advertising although the number and duration of our agreements with advertisers will vary. Commercialisation lettings are also excluded from the void calculation.

The weighted average of the unexpired term of all leases other than short-term lettings such as car parks and advertising hoardings, temporary lettings of less than one year, residential leases and long ground leases.
